## 1. Subordinate clauses

Apart from a few particular cases, subordinate clauses are introduced by these LINKING WORDS which we are beginning to know, thanks to frequent contact with them. These SUBORDINATING words are:

- either *subordinating conjunctions* indicating, among others: CAUSE: quod, quia, *because*; quoniam, *since*… etc.; PURPOSE: ut, *so that*…; ne, *so that… not*, etc.; CONDITION: si…; TIME: antequam, *before*; dum, *while*; postquam, *after*, etc.; COMPARISON: sic… ut, *as*, etc.;
- or *relative words*: PRONOUNS: qui, quae, quod, etc., or ADVERBS: ubi, quo, *there where*…, etc.

A more complete list of these subordinating words, classed by categories, will be found in the GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX.

Subordinates in PERSONAL MOODS (subordinates in the infinitive, the participle and the gerund are not introduced by «subordinating words») can be:

**— either in the indicative**, if it is simply a matter of showing that two FACTS are linked by a simple and natural relation in which the will or the opinion of the subject is not involved. Examples:

- RELATIVE clause: funes qui antemnas destinabant (L. 90, P. 4);
- CAUSAL clause: otium est quoniam exeundi potestas data est (L. 88, P. 3);
- TEMPORAL clause: cum naves circumsteterant milites transcendebant (L. 90, P. 8).

**— or in the subjunctive:**

a) if the will or the opinion of the subject have an influence on the relation of subordination:

> accusatus est quod maledicta in magistratum conjecisset (subj. p.q.p.)

CAUSAL clause where the subjunctive indicates that it is a question of the opinion of the authority, and that this opinion may be wrong; if the insults were an indisputable real fact, one would put conjecerat (ind. p.q.p.) (N.B. — For the sense of the words, see E. 86);

b) if the sense of the subordinate requires it:

> non satis constabat quid agerent (corresponds to a French conditional) (L. 90, P. 2).

N.B. — Note that the same goes for the verb of a main clause;

c) if the subordinating word is always constructed with the subjunctive:

> cave ne cadas, *take care not to fall*

in this case, there is no need to think, for ne is only used with the subjunctive.

If you wish to go deeper into the question, you will find in the GRAMMATICAL APPENDIX:

- the moods used with the different conjunctions, some of which can moreover command, according to their use, either the indicative or the subjunctive (cf. L. 90, N. 18);
- some general indications on the use of moods and tenses (sequence of tenses, etc.);
- some examples of the principal types of subordinate clauses;
- some information on indirect speech (subordinates in the infinitive or in the subjunctive).

## 2. Prefixes (end)

Here now are a few so-called INSEPARABLE prefixes (which are not used as prepositions):

| Prefix | Idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| dis- | dispersion | dissentire (vid. E. 88, P. 12) |
| in- = ne | negation, contrary (not to be confused with in, preposition, *in, on*, etc.) | insanus, *mad*, the opposite of sanus, *sound of body and mind* |
| re- | repetition; return or opposition | reficere, *to repair, to redo*; repugnare, *to repel by fighting* (pugnare) |
| se- or sed- | separation | seducere, *to lead away from the right road, to seduce*; seditio (sed + itio, *action of going*), *disunion, sedition* |

## 3. Suffixes

Just as it is possible to make the sense of certain words more precise by preceding them with a prefix, so it is possible to form new words by adding to existing words an appropriate ending. This possibility must be known by modern Latinists, for they may need it when the dictionary fails them. But they must only use it advisedly, for too often the hasty creation of a new word brings nothing but a new source of confusion (cf. L. 59, remark at the end).

### a) Diminutives

-ellus, -olus, -ulus (-a, -um). E.g.: mus, muris, *the rat*; musculus, *the little rat*, or *the muscle*. — asinus, *the donkey*; asellus, *the little donkey*. — filius, *the son*; filiolus, *the son in infancy, the dear son*.

### b) Nouns (abstract, of profession, etc.)

E.g.: From struere, *to arrange, to assemble*, one can form the following nouns: structor, -oris, m., *the builder*; (con)structio, -onis, f., *the fact of building*; structura, -ae, f., *the result of the assembly, the structure*.

Other examples: vanitas, vanitatis, f., *vanity* (from vanus, *vain*); consuetudo, -inis, f., *habit, custom* (from consuescere, *to get used to*); audacia, -ae, f. (from audax, -acis, *audacious*); decessus, -us, m., *ebb* (from decedere, *to withdraw*); tramen, -inis, n., *the train* (from trahere, *to drag*); atramentum, -i, n., *ink* (from ater, *matt black*); etc.

These derived words present at least one advantage: their gender is automatically given by their ending. Thus -tio, -tas, -tudo are feminine; -or, -us are masculine; -men, -mentum are neuter. Check however that it is indeed derived words in the spirit indicated above for, for example, optio, -onis, *the adjutant*, is masculine; marmor, *the marble*, is neuter; manus is feminine, etc.

### c) Adjectives

Most adjectives are derived words formed with the help of suffixes such as:

| Suffix | Indicates | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -ax, -acis | the (excessive) inclination | loquax, *chatterbox*, from loqui |
| -ilis, -e (or -bilis) | the possibility | missilis, *which can be thrown* (missile), from mittere; possibilis, etc. |
| -eus, -ea, -eum | the material | ferreus, *of iron*, from ferrum; likewise aureus, *of gold*, argenteus, *of silver*, cupreus, *of copper* |
| -osus, -a, -um | abundance | copiosus, *abundant*, from copia, *abundance*; arenosus, *sandy*, from arena, *sand*… |
| -ensis, -is, -e | the inhabitant of… | Amstelodamensis, *of Amsterdam* (Amstelodamum) |
| -idus | the state | cupidus, *who desires* (cupid) from cupere, *to desire*; avidus (cf. L. 80, N. 8); callidus, *cunning, crafty*, and calidus, *hot*; stupidus, etc. |
| -orius | the relation with the action | aleatorius, -a, -um, *relating to games of chance* (aleatory) from alea, -ae, f. (*the die to play with*) |

**Example:** Let us solve the problem: «How do you say LIFT in Latin?». — The root of the French word (*ascenseur*) puts us on the track: scandere, *to climb*. We are therefore going to try to form a word from this verb, and more precisely from its supine scansum, for we have noticed that it is above all from the supine (or the perfect participle for passive verbs) that derivatives are formed. Thus we could take the noun scansor; but we have just seen that derivatives in -or are masculine; they represent the MEN who do the action: scansor is therefore a man who climbs, and not a machine. So we will prefer to use the adjective scansorius, -a, -um, *relating to climbing*. But as an adjective cannot live alone, we must either add a noun to it: pegma scansorium, or cella scansoria (cf. L. 45 and L. 46), or replace it by a noun. Now we have already noticed that the NEUTER form of an adjective could be used as a noun to designate «the thing which has such a quality» (e.g. mala, *bad things, evils*). We can therefore use: scansorium, -ii, n., *the thing relating to climbing*.

**Verification:** The dictionary of BACCI (see Index) gives: pegma scansorium, cellula scansoria, machina scansoria, and anabathrum, a word of Greek origin (p. 59, *ascensore*).

**Conclusion:** By using scansorium alone, we risk at most committing a fault, admissible in familiar conversation, that we commit by saying «an automobile» when we ought to say «an automobile car».

### d) Verbs

One can also form verbs from other words, or else make the sense of existing verbs more precise, with the help of appropriate verbal endings or suffixes:

- VERBS indicating the action of realizing what the word of origin implies. E.g.: liberare, *to free, to make free*, from liber, -era, -erum, *free*; machinari (L. 86, P. 10), from machina; moderari, *to direct (an enterprise)*, from modus, as well as modulari, *to modulate* (music, radio), comes from its derivative modulus, *(small) measure*; ratiocinari, *to reason*, from ratio; sermocinari, *to speak, to sermonize*, from sermo, *speech*. N.B. — Note that these verbs belong to the 1st conjugation (active or deponent).
- INCHOATIVE VERBS (from inchoare, *to begin*), indicating the entry into a state. E.g.: lucesco, -is, -ere, luxi, *to begin to shine*, from luceo, -es, -ere, luxi. Note that the perfects of the two verbs are identical, which is easily understood, for, in the series of the perfectum, two different verbs would make a double use.
- FREQUENTATIVE VERBS, indicating repetition. E.g.: jactare, from jacere (cf. L. 86, N. 4); agitare, from agere (L. 48, N. 9).
- DESIDERATIVE VERBS, indicating a desire or a need. E.g.: esurire, *to need to eat (to be hungry)* from edere (supine esum).

NOTE. — The lists above are very incomplete. You can take advantage of your reading to make new discoveries, which will have the attraction of personal discoveries; but you can also consult specialized works, such as those we have indicated in the BIBLIOGRAPHICAL INDEX (p. 545).
